newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland's PM says balanced 1998 budget impossible.
newsitem.headline: Poland's PM says balanced 1998 budget impossible.

text.p: Polish Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz said on Tuesday a balanced budget was impossible next year.
He was commenting on an earlier statement by the deputy central bank president that only by balancing the 1998 budget could Poland avoid a Czech-style financial crisis.

"There is no such a possibility, in Poland it would require deep budget spending cuts and I do not see such a possibility," Cimoszewicz told Reuters, when asked whether achieving a balanced budget next year was plausible.

Earlier on Tuesday the Rzeczpospolita daily quoted NBP's Witold Kozinski as saying that Poland would have to get rid of the budget deficit, planned at 2.8 percent of GDP this year, to prevent its trade deficit from widening to unacceptable levels.

Cimoszewicz said that Poland needed to cool booming domestic demand to get the trade and current deficit under control, but said that he believed the National Bank of Poland still had instruments at hand to achieve this.

"It is obvious that we have to limit internal demand, which is rapidly growing, but my feeling is that the NBP has instruments to cool it through continuing such measures as increasing mandatory reserves for banks or imposing credit ceilings," Cimoszewicz said after the cabinet meeting.
Asked whether Poland faced the same kind of crisis as the Czech republic where a gaping current account deficit forced the authorities to take tough measures to restore the balance, Cimoszewicz said:
"I don't think so, of course there are no guarantees (that such a crisis will not happen) becuase it depends on what sort of policy the government undertakes."
Cimoszewicz added that the Czech Republic had a roughly balanced budget and still fell into financial trouble.

NBP predicted that if the budget deficit was reduced to 1.7 percent of GDP and growth maintained at 5.5 percent, the trade deficit would jump to $16 billion from $12 billion predicted for 1997, reaching a dangerously high proportion of GDP.
Finance Minister Marek Belka has said the government would seek much tighter budget next year and signalled the deficit would be at or below two percent, but so far had not given specific figures.
